title: Deep repertoire, avoiding nostalgia, and a dinner interruption
summary: Herman picks material to suit the audience, using Nat Pierce charts at dance dates; Mrs. Herman interrupts about leftovers.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: You, of course, like many people -- not many, I can't say that, bandleaders that have such a deep repertory, so many decades of experience, and a number of selections associated with you specifically. It gives you a breadth of material to choose from, whenever you want to. You would 'Laura' if you wanted to, or something that's -- you just did a week ago. And you can mix that up. And most people can't do that. And you don't do anything for nostalgia purposes, either, do you?
Well, I try not, but however, we're all
kind of guided by the people we're playing for, and if it's an older audience you're going to play other things that you would for --
Sure. I know, when you do a dance date, you have a lot of Nat Pierce's charts, "Deep Purple."
(Inaudible) leftovers. Is that okay with you guys?
I can't take it, I'm going out.
